## The idea

Correct chords do not guarantee a clear arrangement. When two voices occupy a
similar pitch range, use comparable envelopes, and sit in the same stereo
position, their identities can blur even if every note belongs to the harmony.
Lowering one part changes the balance, but the quieter sound may continue to
mask or be masked in the same region.

Three dimensions offer more informative choices. *Register* means pitch
height. *Timbre* is the spectral character that distinguishes, for example, a
hollow sustained tone from a bright pluck. Space includes stereo position and
the apparent depth produced by direct sound and reflections. Move a part an
octave, shorten its envelope, pan it away from a neighbour, or use reverb to
place it behind a drier foreground.

Leave volume for the final balance pass. First each musical role needs a
place where the ear can identify its attacks and follow its continuation. Once
those places exist, amplitude can decide which role stands forward without
having to compensate for unresolved overlap.

## Run this

One four-chord skeleton receives three treatments. The sparse pass states only a
low root and high chord tone. The dense pass piles one saw voicing and a second
copy transposed three semitones higher into the middle, changing pitch classes as
well as density. The wide pass separates a sustained low voice from a high, short
pluck and gives each a distinct stereo and depth position.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 78

progression = [
  chord(:c3, :minor),
  chord(:ab2, :major),
  chord(:eb3, :major),
  chord(:bb2, :major)
]

define :render_skeleton do |chords, layout|
  chords.each do |notes|
    if layout == :sparse
      use_synth :piano
      play notes.first, release: 1.8, amp: 0.7
      play notes.last + 12, release: 1.2, amp: 0.6
    elsif layout == :dense
      use_synth :saw
      play_chord notes.map { |pitch| pitch + 12 }, release: 1.8, amp: 0.55
      play_chord notes.map { |pitch| pitch + 15 }, release: 1.8, amp: 0.5
    else
      with_fx :reverb, room: 0.7, mix: 0.35 do
        use_synth :hollow
        play notes.first, release: 2.4, amp: 0.55, pan: -0.5
      end
      use_synth :pluck
      play notes.last + 24, release: 0.7, amp: 0.65, pan: 0.55
    end
    sleep 2
  end
end

render_skeleton progression, :sparse
sleep 1
render_skeleton progression, :dense
sleep 1
render_skeleton progression, :wide
```

In the dense pass, related saw spectra and the added transposition occupy much of
the same band. Listen for whether that overlap makes individual tones harder to
trace. The wide pass schedules a low sustain on the left and a high pluck on the
right; audition is still needed to determine how clearly register, envelope, pan,
and reverb separate those roles on a particular playback system.

## Change one thing

1. Remove `+ 24` from the pluck in the wide layout. Its attacks fall toward the
   sustained part's register while the stereo positions remain separated.
   Listen for pitch identity becoming less distinct; pan can locate two sounds
   horizontally without preventing their spectra from competing.
2. Restore the octave shift and set both pans to 0. Register and envelope still
   distinguish the centred parts. This comparison reveals how much separation
   survives when stereo position stops contributing.
3. Raise the reverb mix to 0.75. The sustained voice recedes and its direct
   attack loses definition as reflections become more prominent. Return to
   0.35 before adding any echo to the pluck, so depth changes remain attributable
   to one effect at a time.

## Why it works

*Masking* occurs when sounds make one another harder to perceive because they
occupy similar frequency bands at similar times. Register separation reduces
some of that spectral overlap. Contrasting envelopes keep attacks and sustains
from competing continuously. Panning provides interaural level and timing cues,
while reverb changes the balance between direct and reflected sound and thus
the apparent distance of a source.

The dimensions interact. Moving a saw's fundamental downward does not remove
its many upper partials from the middle register. A sine-like bass may leave
more space above it. Likewise, a short release can open useful gaps, but a long
reverb tail may immediately refill them. Change one dimension, listen for the
specific collision it addresses, and then decide whether another dimension is
still needed.

The harmonic skeleton remains input data; `layout` controls rendering. All three
versions receive the same chord records in the same order, but the dense renderer
adds three semitones rather than an octave and therefore changes the pitch-class
content. Its cloudiness cannot be attributed to layout alone. Replace `+ 15`
with `+ 12` or `+ 24` when you want a controlled comparison that preserves the
harmony and varies only register, density, and sound design.

Depth is relational. A reverberant voice sounds distant because a drier voice
provides a foreground against which to hear it. If every part uses the same
large room and wet mix, the whole image recedes together and the distinction
disappears. Audition the layout on headphones and speakers at a moderate level;
stereo cues and low-frequency response can differ enough to expose a collision
that one playback system concealed.

## Take it further

Arrange the same eight-bar harmonic skeleton in sparse, dense, and wide
versions, leaving the chord data untouched. Use two roles in the sparse
arrangement and at least four in the dense one. In the wide version, distinguish
each role from its nearest neighbour along two dimensions chosen from register,
synth, envelope, pan, and effect depth. For every collision you hear, write a
one-line diagnosis that names the competing roles and dimension. Address the
collision without changing chord roots or reaching first for the master level.
